26.0.0.en: 1 And it came to pass in the eleventh year, in the first day of the month, that the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 2 “Son of man, because that Tyrus hath said against Jerusalem, Aha, she is broken that was the gates of the people: she is turned unto me: I shall be replenished, now she is laid waste:

26.0.1.en: Tyre is a famous Phoenician city that appeared around 2750 B.C. on the mainland, but with time, for defensive reasons, it was moved to a neighboring rocky island bearing the same name, with an area of 142 acres and having two harbors. It is nearer to the children of Israel than Sidon and surpasses it in greatness; the Hebrews did not occupy it in the days of Joshua. Its king sent building materials to King David (2 Sam 15:11) and to Solomon the Wise (1 Kgs 9:10-14). The Tyrians delivered the children of Israel to Edom (Amos 1:9), stripped them of their goods, and sold them as slaves to the Greeks (Joel 3:5-6). Nebuchadnezzar besieged them for 13 years (585-573 B.C.), and finally she negotiated with him and acknowledged his authority. Alexander the Great also besieged it and occupied it in 332 B.C. Yet it soon regained its glory, and after his death it fell under the assault of the Seleucids, and then the Romans took it from them.

26.0.2.en: The Lord Christ passed by its shores (Mt 15:21-28; Mk 7:24-31), and people from Tyre also came to Him (Mk 3:8; Lk 6:17). Christianity entered it in the apostolic age (Acts 21:3-4), and Origen was buried in the basilica at Tyre, where St. Paulinus built a magnificent church, in which Eusebius the historian delivered a sermon on the day of its consecration in the year 323. In the fourth century St. Jerome described it as the most honorable and the most beautiful of the cities of Phoenicia, and said that it trades with the whole world. It was distinguished above all the bishoprics of the See of Antioch after Antioch itself, and its head used to hand the pastoral staff to the Patriarch at his enthronement.

26.0.3.en: As for the name “Tyre,” it is a Semitic name meaning “rock,” perhaps because it was established on a rocky island; yet St. Jerome holds that the word “Tyre” in Hebrew means “distress,” and therefore he sees its inhabitants as representing those who fall under the distress and plagues of Satan.

26.0.4.en: In any case, this prophecy (Ezek 26) came against Tyre in the eleventh year, on the first of the month, that is, after the destruction of Jerusalem, but no news had reached him and the captives in the first phase, for he learned of it in the twelfth year, in the tenth month, on the fifth of the month (Ezek 33:21).

26.1.0.en: The sin of Tyre is covetousness, in that she exploited the destruction of Jerusalem; she gloated, saying: “Aha, she is broken that was the gates of the people: she is turned unto me: I shall be replenished, now she is laid waste” [2]. Jerusalem was like the gates of the peoples in one of two senses: either she was strong like closed gates which the peoples could not overcome, and now she has become wide open and ruined, trodden by all, open to Tyre as to the other peoples; or she (Jerusalem) was a center of world trade, and by her destruction the way opened for Tyre to seize all her customers and grow rich at her expense, because Tyre lived by trade.

26.2.0.en: 3 Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I am against thee, O Tyrus, and will cause many nations to come up against thee, as the sea causeth his waves to come up. 4 And they shall destroy the walls of Tyrus, and break down her towers: I will also scrape her dust from her, and make her like the top of a rock. 5 It shall be a place for the spreading of nets in the midst of the sea: for I have spoken it, saith the Lord GOD: and it shall become a spoil to the nations. 6 And her daughters which are in the field shall be slain by the sword; and they shall know that I am the LORD.

26.2.1.en: Since she coveted Jerusalem, she exploited its ruin in order to be filled, rejoicing and exulting in seizing this opportunity; therefore God Himself stands against her and stirs up the nations against her, as the sea sends its waves without ceasing. He speaks to her in the language that Tyre understands, as an island in the midst of the sea. She imagined that by the destruction of Jerusalem ships would come to her from all the world seeking her wares, and she would grow rich; but behold, instead of sending its ships the sea sends her its waves, destroying her walls, breaking down her towers, scraping her dust from her, and making her a completely bare rock.

26.2.2.en: She rejoiced because the closed gates of Jerusalem were opened to her by force; behold, Tyre herself has become without walls, gates or towers, indeed without dust, a rock unfit for life, which no man inhabits, no animal rests upon, and no plant grows upon. Truly, he who thinks of his brother that he is a prey for himself, the Lord makes him a prey for others, indeed makes him altogether useless for anything! This is the fruit of covetousness in a man’s life!

26.3.0.en: 7 “For thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I will bring upon Tyrus Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, a king of kings, from the north, with horses, and with chariots, and with horsemen, and companies, and much people. 8 He shall slay with the sword thy daughters in the field: and he shall make a fort against thee, and cast a mount against thee, and lift up the buckler against thee. 9 And he shall set engines of war against thy walls, and with his axes he shall break down thy towers. 10 By reason of the abundance of his horses their dust shall cover thee: thy walls shall shake at the noise of the horsemen, and of the wheels, and of the chariots, when he shall enter into thy gates, as men enter into a city wherein is made a breach. 11 With the hoofs of his horses shall he tread down all thy streets: he shall slay thy people by the sword, and thy strong garrisons shall go down to the ground. 12 And they shall make a spoil of thy riches, and make a prey of thy merchandise: and they shall break down thy walls, and destroy thy pleasant houses: and they shall lay thy stones and thy timber and thy dust in the midst of the water. 13 And I will cause the noise of thy songs to cease; and the sound of thy harps shall be no more heard. 14 And I will make thee like the top of a rock: thou shalt be a place to spread nets upon; thou shalt be built no more: for I the LORD have spoken it, saith the Lord GOD.

26.3.1.en: If Nebuchadnezzar shattered Jerusalem, he also besieged Tyre with his army for thirteen years until he conquered it. She became a prey for him and his army, and the prophet pictured the state of Tyre, which coveted Jerusalem, in the following points:

26.4.0.en: A. He slays her daughters [8]; perhaps here he means the killing of her customers who come from all the world to trade with her... The daughters symbolize the works of the flesh and its fruit, for the man who gloats over his brother becomes fruitless. Instead of Tyre gaining from behind Jerusalem, she loses every material fruit!

26.4.1.en: B. By the multitude of his army and his horses he covers her with their dust, so that she loses all sight and forfeits all her beauty, and her merchants no longer come to her.

26.5.0.en: C. He slays her people by the sword, and the pillars of her strength go down to the ground [11]. This is a sign of the slaying of her people and her leaders, who fall from glory and honor to the dust.

26.5.1.en: D. They make a spoil of her riches and prey of her merchandise, and break down her walls and her pleasant houses, and lay her stones and her timber and her dust in the midst of the water, so that she becomes a rock utterly bare of everything, even of dust!

26.6.0.en: E. He causes her songs, the sound of the harp and joy to cease [13].

26.6.1.en: This is the work of covetousness: not only does a man lose what he coveted, but he loses his wealth, his strength, his beauty, his joy and his health, and loses others, and becomes stripped of his humanity and of all vitality in him!

26.6.2.en: Tyre thought that she would acquire many gains by the destruction of Jerusalem, but behold, she enters not only into material losses but loses her sons and daughters.

26.6.3.en: She reckoned that she would become the object of the world’s concern through the annihilation of Jerusalem, but behold, the armies surround her, the dust covers her, and all mock her.

26.6.4.en: She awaits honor and greatness through the collapse of Jerusalem, but her people are slain together with their leaders...

26.6.5.en: Instead of the gains she foretells through the destruction of Jerusalem, she becomes a spoil for her plunderers, loses all her security, her beauty vanishes, and she is turned into a bare rock.

26.6.6.en: She had been singing and dancing with delight at the destruction of Jerusalem, and joy and gladness were taken from her!

26.7.0.en: 15 “Thus saith the Lord GOD to Tyrus; Shall not the isles shake at the sound of thy fall, when the wounded cry, when the slaughter is made in the midst of thee? 16 Then all the princes of the sea shall come down from their thrones, and lay away their robes, and put off their broidered garments: they shall clothe themselves with trembling; they shall sit upon the ground, and shall tremble at every moment, and be astonished at thee. 17 And they shall take up a lamentation for thee, and say to thee, How art thou destroyed, that wast inhabited of seafaring men, the renowned city, which wast strong in the sea, she and her inhabitants, which cause their terror to be on all that haunt it! 18 Now shall the isles tremble in the day of thy fall; yea, the isles that are in the sea shall be troubled at thy departure. 19 For thus saith the Lord GOD; When I shall make thee a desolate city, like the cities that are not inhabited; when I shall bring up the deep upon thee, and great waters shall cover thee, “Shall not the isles shake at the sound of thy fall, when the wounded cry, when the slaughter is made in the midst of thee? Then all the princes of the sea shall come down from their thrones, and lay away their robes, and put off their broidered garments: they shall clothe themselves with trembling; they shall sit upon the ground, and shall tremble at every moment, and be astonished at thee, and they shall take up a lamentation for thee” [15-17].

26.7.1.en: The collapse of Tyre shakes the rest of the isles, for they had thought that this rich and famous island, which stands like a rock in the midst of the sea, could not be defeated or conquered by anyone. Tyre has collapsed, so what will the small lands do?! There is no need to fight them; rather the princes come down from their thrones in fear and put off the garments of kingship, trembling clothes them, and they sit on the ground in fear and bewilderment! They take up a lamentation over Tyre while in reality they are weeping for their own condition!

26.7.2.en: Ananias and Sapphira fell and died because they were covetous; they lied to the Holy Spirit and kept back part of the price of the land (Acts 5:3), and great fear came upon all who heard of it. They became like covetous Tyre, and lost their lives together with their possessions and became an example to others.

26.7.3.en: Perhaps these isles refer to the merchants who came to her to deal with her, or to the ships coming carrying goods from all the world... They offer a lamentation over Tyre, the center of trade. How marvelous: when Jerusalem, the city of the Great King, fell, she found no one to lament for her, but found those who mocked and reproached her; but as for Tyre, when she was ruined the isles rose up to lament her. Jerusalem fell, but the Lord raised her up after she had been disciplined; but Tyre fell and the world lamented her, yet she did not rise but vanished forever! Thus the believer falls under discipline and there is no one to pity him, yet the eye of the Lord has compassion on him and supports him; but the wicked man who is determined in his evil, when he falls many lament him, yet he does not rise! And perhaps by this he meant “evil” itself, which falls and does not rise.

26.8.0.en: 20 “When I shall bring thee down with them that descend into the pit, with the people of old time, and shall set thee in the low parts of the earth, in places desolate of old, with them that go down to the pit, that thou be not inhabited; and I shall set glory in the land of the living; 21 I will make thee a terror, and thou shalt be no more: though thou be sought for, yet shalt thou never be found again, saith the Lord GOD.” [20-21].

26.8.1.en: If Tyre represents the sin of covetousness, then although at the beginning it appears bright and attractive and many desire it, it is deceitful; it perishes and no longer exists. It is like all other sins: a man thinks that in it lies all his satisfaction, his pleasure and his happiness, but he soon discovers that it does not exist. It is like a mirage that a man runs after and is never quenched!

26.8.2.en: Let her fall that I may be enriched!

26.8.3.en: * Let her fall that I myself may be enriched!

26.8.4.en: This is what Tyre sang when Jerusalem collapsed!

26.8.5.en: She is a gloating, covetous one, at the expense of others!

26.8.6.en: * What, I wonder, did Tyre gain by the destruction of Jerusalem?

26.8.7.en: Instead of gaining merchants she lost her daughters; instead of the world being occupied with her alone she became the spoil of armies; instead of obtaining honor her people were slain; and instead of joy and singing she became a bare, wretched rock!

26.8.8.en: * Teach me, O Lord, love and mercy, that I may not gloat over the misfortunes of my brethren, nor exploit these opportunities for my own benefit!

26.8.9.en: Remove Tyre from my heart, and grant me to be poured out for my brethren, sharing their feelings, and counting them my joy and my crown!

27.0.0.en: 1 The word of the LORD came again unto me, saying, 2 “Now, thou son of man, take up a lamentation for Tyrus; 3 And say unto Tyrus, O thou that art situate at the entry of the sea, which art a merchant of the people for many isles, Thus saith the Lord GOD; O Tyrus, thou hast said, I am of perfect beauty. 4 Thy borders are in the midst of the seas, thy builders have perfected thy beauty. 5 They have made all thy ship boards of fir trees of Senir: they have taken cedars from Lebanon to make masts for thee. 6 Of the oaks of Bashan have they made thine oars; the company of the Ashurites have made thy benches of ivory, brought out of the isles of Chittim. 7 Fine linen with broidered work from Egypt was that which thou spreadest forth to be thy sail; blue and purple from the isles of Elishah was that which covered thee. 8 The inhabitants of Zidon and Arvad were thy mariners: thy wise men, O Tyrus, that were in thee, were thy pilots. 9 The ancients of Gebal and the wise men thereof were in thee thy calkers: all the ships of the sea with their mariners were in thee to occupy thy merchandise. 10 They of Persia and of Lud and of Phut were in thine army, thy men of war: they hanged the shield and helmet in thee; they set forth thy comeliness. 11 The men of Arvad with thine army were upon thy walls round about, and the Gammadims were in thy towers: they hanged their shields upon thy walls round about; they have made thy beauty perfect.

27.0.1.en: If Jerusalem refers to the soul that has received the grace of God (in the Old Testament it refers to the Church enjoying the Mosaic Law and the prophets, and in the New Testament it refers to the Church that has enjoyed eternal salvation through divine grace in Christ Jesus), then Tyre here represents natural man: his position, his resources and the gifts God gave him, and then his fall and collapse through sin. So what is said here of Tyre is said of the whole of human nature. He likened it to a Phoenician ship in an excellent location, dealing with many peoples, strongly built, exceedingly precious, magnificent in its workmanship, with an excellent crew, lacking nothing. This is man, “the work of the hands of God, the Lover of mankind.”

27.1.0.en: God established her “at the entry of the sea,” for Tyre lies in the east of the Mediterranean Sea as a beautiful island with two harbors, and its location enables it to draw merchants from all the lands of the East; “a merchant of the people for many isles” [3], “thy borders are in the midst of the seas” [4]. God established man at the entries of the seas, “above every earthly creature,” being in the image of God, so that he has dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth (Gen 1:26). He entrusted this trade to him that he might be a master, not a slave, of earthly and temporal things; He set his borders in all the seas, that is, he is the possessor of authority over everything. He did not want to create us to live in material or psychological deprivation, but wanted for us satisfaction in everything.

27.1.1.en: As St. Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, says: [In his treatise on the creation, God did not create man until He had created the world as a royal palace, for it is not fitting to proclaim the king until his palace is made ready.]

27.2.0.en: God established man beautiful in everything, the perfection of His creation on earth; therefore after He created him it was said: “And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good” (Gen 1:31)... And the lamentation says: “Thy builders have perfected thy beauty” [4]; the secret of our beauty is God, who built our life and gave us the inner resources and the body as a free gift from Him. But man, in pride receiving it, instead of thanking God and glorifying Him, ascribes all perfection to himself, for the lamentation says: “O Tyrus, thou hast said, I am of perfect beauty” [3].

27.2.1.en: And the secret of her beauty is:

27.2.2.en: Her boards are of fir trees of Senir, her masts of the cedars of Lebanon, her oars of the oaks of Bashan, her benches of ivory inlaid in box, from the isles of Chittim.

27.2.3.en: Her sail is fine linen with broidered work from Egypt, her covering is blue and purple from the isles of Elishah.

27.2.4.en: Her mariners are from the people of Zidon and Arvad, her pilots are wise men of Tyre itself, her calkers are the ancients of Gebal and its wise men, her men of war (her guards) are from Persia, Lud and Phut...

27.2.5.en: Thus the lamentation presented many details of the building materials of the ship and the nationality of its crew and its guards. It must be observed that among the Gentiles the ship often refers to the journey of life which man lives in the world in order to enter the harbor, just as Noah’s ark symbolized the Church or humanity enjoying divine salvation; therefore churches are often built in the shape of a ship. As Father Hippolytus says: [The sea is the world; the Church went down into it to the very depth, yet she did not perish, because her captain, Christ, is skilled. Since she bears the Cross of the Lord, she bears within her the victory over death...

27.2.6.en: The sailors are the two Testaments (the Old and the New).

27.2.7.en: And the mountains surrounding her are the love of Christ which binds the Church.

27.2.8.en: The net that is with her is the font of the new birth which renews the believers.

27.2.9.en: The Holy Spirit dwells in her as a skilled sailor, by whom the believers are sealed...

27.2.10.en: She has anchors of iron that hold her, which are the commandments of Christ Himself, strong as iron!

27.2.11.en: In her are seamen on the right and on the left, servants like the holy angels who steer the Church and guard her.

27.2.12.en: The ladder by which we go up to the deck of the ship is the remembrance of the sufferings of Christ, by which the hearts of the believers are raised to heaven.

27.2.13.en: The towers upon the ship are the fellowship of the prophets, martyrs and apostles who enter into their rest...]

27.2.14.en: And as the ship refers to humanity renewed through the Cross of Christ, it also refers to human nature before the fall; therefore what is stated in the lamentation in the way of details refers to God’s gifts to us through our humanity: a good body, a rational soul, emotions, feelings, inclinations, drives and blessed energies, because they are the work of the hands of the good God, the Lover of mankind.

27.2.15.en: We can say that the boards or beams of the ship are the members of the body, its mast is the mind, the oar is the tongue, the benches are the rest of the senses, the sail is the heart, the covering is outward conduct, the mariners are the inner energies of the soul, its pilot is the spirit of discernment and distinction, the calkers are the gifts, and the guards are the inner drives.

27.2.16.en: A. All the boards are of fir trees of Senir, that is, all the members of the body, which are like the beams of the ship, come from the mountain of light (Senir), and not, as the Gnostics thought, from the kingdom of darkness. Therefore the Fathers often dealt with this matter, and St. John Chrysostom says: [These (the followers of Mani) call the body treacherous, of an evil origin... Would this not oblige them to pluck out their eyes, because desire enters the soul by way of them?! But the truth is that it is not the eye nor any other member that is to be blamed, but our corrupt will alone is the object of blame.] He also says: [Eyes were given to us that we might look with them at creation and so glorify the Lord, but if we misuse them they become servants of fornication...] And St. Augustine says: [The spirit is good, and the body is good. And man, who is composed of the two, is certainly good, whether this goodness of his be little or much.]

27.2.17.en: B. The mast, that is, the mind, is taken from the cedars of Lebanon, which is known for its uprightness; for God created for man an upright mind that leads him all the way without deviation, since “the truly rational man has only one concern, which is to obey Almighty God with all his heart and to please Him, and he teaches himself only one thing, which is how to do, as far as he can, what agrees with God, thanking Him for His compassionate providence that works in everything that happens to him in his life.”

27.2.18.en: C. The oar that steers the ship is the tongue, for our teacher James says: “Behold also the ships, which though they be so great, and are driven of fierce winds, yet are they turned about with a very small helm, whithersoever the governor listeth. Even so the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things” (Jas 3:4-5). And St. John Chrysostom says: [We were given a tongue to teach and praise the Creator with it, but if we do not take heed to ourselves it becomes a cause of blasphemy.]

27.2.19.en: D. The benches are the senses, which ought to be of inlaid ivory, that is, full of purity and cleanness. St. John Saba says: [Everyone who now wishes to keep his soul and his conscience from evil deeds, let him guard these senses and deliver them into the hand of the faithful God, the Helper of the weak.]

27.2.20.en: E. The sail is the heart, which ought to be of embroidered linen, clean and pure; for when the heart is sanctified man becomes a dwelling for God, and therefore the psalmist cries: “Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me” (Ps 51).

27.2.21.en: F. The covering of the ship, which is conduct, is of blue, that is, bearing the heavenly nature, and of purple, that is, bearing the mark of kings. For conduct expresses what the heart bears within; if the heart is lifted up to heaven, where our treasure is, our conduct also is directed toward heavenly things, and where it is with God, the true King, the conduct is worthy of the children of this King. Therefore the Apostle Paul says: “[He] hath raised us up together, and made us sit together in heavenly places.”

27.2.22.en: “Seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God” (Col 3:1).

27.2.23.en: And St. John Climacus says: [Great is he who overcomes the fire arising from earthly pleasures by meditation on the delights of heaven!]

27.2.24.en: G. The mariners, that is, the inner energies of the soul, he brings from Zidon and Arvad. If “Zidon” means “place of hunting,” then the living man is the one who uses all his inner energies for building, living as a skilled hunter who knows how to acquire what is for edification. If they are not used for edification, these same energies become for demolition, and if they are not like spiritual soldiers on behalf of the Kingdom of God they become like wicked soldiers on behalf of the kingdom of darkness.

27.2.25.en: H. Her pilot, who is the spirit of distinction or discernment, is from Tyre, that is, like the rock he is not shaken. This is the secret of the strength of the spiritual man: he walks with discernment, knowing how to separate good from evil, truth from falsehood, light from darkness. So he accepts what is for his edification and rejects what is for demolition with strength, without moving.

27.2.26.en: I. The calkers, that is, the gifts, are from the ancients of Gebal and its wise men. For God has given each man special gifts which he kindles with power and wisdom, so that they are in him like wise elders, working together with the gifts of others for the edification of humanity as one family.

27.2.27.en: J. As for her guards, who are the inner drives of the soul, they are from Persia, Lud and Phut, men of war, trained and of varied experience, working to protect her. Among these drives are anger, fear, motherhood, fatherhood, love, etc... All these are holy drives if they work within the spiritual framework of edification. For through anger a man rises up against sin and blames himself, through fear he reveres God and does not wound His feelings, and through motherhood, fatherhood and love he gathers in his heart a pure love toward humanity in the spirit of wisdom that is not rash. These are the men of war within the soul, who fight either for us or against us. He who is angry at others and not at himself, and who fears men and not God, and who loves for the sake of fleshly desire, turns the men of war against himself.

27.2.28.en: This is a swift and brief picture of the ship “of perfect beauty” which God gave us, that is, human nature before its deviation and fall!

27.3.0.en: 12 Tarshish was thy merchant by reason of the multitude of all kind of riches; with silver, iron, tin, and lead, they traded in thy fairs. 13 Javan, Tubal, and Meshech, they were thy merchants: they traded the persons of men and vessels of brass in thy market. 14 They of the house of Togarmah traded in thy fairs with horses and horsemen and mules. 15 The men of Dedan were thy merchants; many isles were the merchandise of thine hand: they brought thee for a present horns of ivory and ebony. 16 Syria was thy merchant by reason of the multitude of the wares of thy making: they occupied in thy fairs with emeralds, purple, and broidered work, and fine linen, and coral, and agate. 17 Judah, and the land of Israel, they were thy merchants: they traded in thy market wheat of Minnith, and Pannag, and honey, and oil, and balm. 18 Damascus was thy merchant in the multitude of the wares of thy making, for the multitude of all riches; in the wine of Helbon, and white wool. 19 Dan also and Javan going to and fro occupied in thy fairs: bright iron, cassia, and calamus, were in thy market. 20 Dedan was thy merchant in precious clothes for chariots. 21 Arabia, and all the princes of Kedar, they occupied with thee in lambs, and rams, and goats: in these were they thy merchants. 22 The merchants of Sheba and Raamah, they were thy merchants: they occupied in thy fairs with chief of all spices, and with all precious stones, and gold. 23 Haran, and Canneh, and Eden, the merchants of Sheba, Asshur, and Chilmad, were thy merchants. 24 These were thy merchants in all sorts of things, in blue clothes, and broidered work, and in chests of rich apparel, bound with cords, and made of cedar, among thy merchandise.

27.3.1.en: After presenting the precious building materials of the ship, its excellent crew and its guards, mighty in experience, he began to speak of its precious cargo, for it was filled with valuable goods which it brought from many lands. It resembles the wise soul that knows how to benefit spiritually from every man, despises no one, and does not depend on its own experience alone. Man is like the bee that knows how to draw from every flower what is sweet and beautiful!

27.3.2.en: In speaking of the goods in which the ship traded, the order came according to the locations of the lands, so he began with the coasts of the Mediterranean Sea, then the eastern lands in three parallel lines from south to north. The following are the lands mentioned and the goods in which they trade.

27.3.3.en: Tarshish: silver, iron, tin and lead.

27.3.4.en: Javan, Tubal and Meshech: slaves and vessels of brass.

27.3.5.en: The house of Togarmah: horses and mules.

27.3.6.en: Dedan, Rhodes or Rodam: ivory and ebony.

27.3.7.en: Aram: emeralds, purple, broidered work, fine linen, coral and agate.

27.3.8.en: Judah and Israel: wheat of Minnith and Pannag (a place name, or perhaps a kind of sweet; perhaps he meant early figs, as in some editions), honey, oil and balm.

27.3.9.en: Damascus: the wine of Helbon and white wool.

27.3.10.en: Dan and Javan: yarn, wrought iron, cassia and calamus.

27.3.12.en: Arabia and Kedar: lambs, rams and goats.

27.3.13.en: Sheba and Raamah: spices, precious stones and gold.

27.3.14.en: Haran, Canneh and Eden: rich blue garments and broidered work, and carpets of rich colors bound with cords made of cedar.

27.3.15.en: This is the list of the lands which trade with Tyre and the goods in which they trade, and the following is a brief outline of some of these lands:

27.3.16.en: Tarshish: this name is probably derived from the word “rashash,” found in the Akkadian language connected with shining metals and the products of mines; therefore this name became famous in the sense of “the refining of metals.”

27.3.17.en: The people of Tarshish came from Javan (Gen 10:4), and it is thought to be Tartessus, situated in the south of Spain near Gibraltar, and perhaps it is Carthage, the city situated in the northwest of Africa. It was very rich in metals such as silver beaten into plates (Jer 10:9), and iron, tin and lead. If Sheba and Dedan represent trade in the East, then Tarshish represents trade in the West; therefore it is said in the prophet Ezekiel: “Sheba, and Dedan, and the merchants of Tarshish, with all the young lions thereof, shall say unto thee, Art thou come to take a spoil? hast thou gathered thy company to take a prey? to carry away silver and gold, to take away cattle and goods, to take a great spoil?” (Ezek 38:13).

27.3.18.en: And when it is said “ships of Tarshish,” it does not necessarily mean that they are ships of the king of Tarshish or that they trade with Tarshish, but because of its commercial fame the name was applied to the huge ocean-crossing ships that sailed especially to bring precious metals.

27.3.19.en: And let us not forget that when the Lord asked Jonah to preach in Nineveh in the East, he fled to the West in a ship sailing to Tarshish (Jon 1:3).

27.3.20.en: Javan: Javan came with Tubal and the far-off isles in (Isa 66:19), where the Gentiles come to it and declare the glory of God, and the sons of the Javanites are mentioned as merchants buying the captives of Judah and Israel to remove them far from their border in (Joel 3:6), and here in (Ezek 27:13) with Tubal and Meshech as merchants of captives, slaves and vessels of brass. These three expressions refer to the Javanite, that is, Greek, colonies on the coast of Asia Minor. It is to be noted that the term Javan, Jonia, is very close to the expression of the Assyrians and Egyptians for “Greece.”

27.3.21.en: Moreover the “Javan” mentioned in (Ezek 27:19) means another Javan, most probably a tribe in Arabia or a Greek colony in Arabia.

27.3.22.en: In (Dan 8:21; 10:20; 11:2) Javan is translated “Greece,” and it most often refers here to the Macedonian Greek empire.

27.3.23.en: Tubal and Meshech: two peoples or regions in Asia Minor, linked together (Isa 66:19), and belonging to Japheth (Gen 10:2; Job 1:5), who appeared in the Assyrian records under the names Tabali and Mushki as fierce opponents of Assyria in the twelfth century B.C.

27.3.24.en: The house of Togarmah: it lies in the south of Armenia, inhabited by the descendants of Togarmah, the third son of Gomer (Gen 10:1; 1 Chr 1:6).

27.4.0.en: Dedan [15]: a people in the north of Arabia, who came from Cush the son of Ham (Gen 10:7), and it is stated in (Gen 25:3) that he was of the offspring of Abraham by Keturah after the death of Sarah. It is not difficult to understand the connection here if we remember the kinship between Arabia and Cush.

27.4.1.en: They were men of trade, from the lands of the Arabs (Isa 21:3), dwelling south of the Edomites (Jer 25:23; 49:8). The name still remains in Didan, southwest of Tema. As for modern Dedan, it is “al-Ula,” an oasis in the Wadi al-Qura in the north of the Hejaz.

27.4.2.en: Aram: taken from the Akkadian and meaning “the high land”; Aram was one of the sons of Shem (Gen 10:22-23). Aram extends from Mount Lebanon in the west to beyond the Euphrates in the east, and from the Taurus mountains in the north to Damascus in the south. This region was called Syria in the Septuagint. Abraham was called “a wandering Aramean” because he went out from Haran [one of the cities of Aram (Gen 11:3) to Canaan (Deut 26:5)]. Several Aramean states appeared, such as Aram of the two rivers (Gen 24:10), in which lie the cities of Nisibis and Edessa, and Aram of Damascus, and Aram-zobah or Zobah west of the Euphrates (which at times extended to the borders of Hamath), and Aram-maacah near Mount Hermon, in the portion of Manasseh (Josh 12:5; 13:11), and Geshur as an Aramean state near Maacah, east of the Jordan also in the portion of Manasseh (Deut 3:14), to which Absalom fled after killing his brother Amnon (2 Sam 13:37; 15:8), and Aram of Beth-rehob, most probably near the entrance of Hamath (Num 13:21; Josh 19:28).

27.4.3.en: Damascus: the capital of Syria, known from ancient times as an important commercial center. It stands at the eastern foot of the Anti-Lebanon, where in this range of mountains the two rivers Abana and Pharpar spring (2 Kgs 5:12), now called Barada and al-Awaj.

27.4.4.en: Dan: a Hebrew name meaning “judge,” a city in the north of the borders of Palestine; it was called Laish (Judg 18:29) or Leshem (Josh 19:47), but it is not, as some think, at Tell al-Qadi. The confusion arose because of the similarity of names, since “Dan” means “judge.”

27.4.5.en: Kedar: a Semitic name meaning “mighty or black,” and he is the second son of Ishmael (Gen 25:13). His descendants for the most part lived by pasturing in black tents, so Kedar became a symbol of the color black (Song 1:5). Some of them were civilized (Isa 42:11). They were owners of cattle and skilled in war, especially in shooting with the bow, and therefore they resisted Nebuchadnezzar greatly, but he made an example of them.

27.4.6.en: Sheba: Sheba and his brother Dan are mentioned as sons of Raamah, of the sons of Cush (Gen 10:7), and the two names are also mentioned as sons of Jokshan the son of Abraham by Keturah his wife (Gen 25:7).

27.4.7.en: Sheba is considered one of four important tribes or ancient peoples who inhabited southern Arabia: the Qatabanians, the Mineans, the Chattramothites (in Hebrew Hazarmaveth), and Sheba, which was the most important of them in the days of Strabo. They were famous as merchants of spices, gold and precious stones, and were very rich. They traded in slaves (Joel 3:8) and were regarded as guardians of the desert (Job 1:15; 6:19).

27.4.8.en: The Assyrian inscriptions have perhaps furnished us with the oldest testimony to the existence of Sheba, for King Tiglathpileser III (745-727 B.C.) recorded the receiving of tribute from Itamara, king of Sheba...

27.4.9.en: It appears that this people, who settled in the southwest of the peninsula (Gen 10:28), had some of their families migrate to Ethiopia (Cush) and were called Cushite (Gen 25:3), and some later extended to the northwest of the peninsula until they reached Syria.

27.4.10.en: The story of the Queen of Sheba gave them special fame, and revealed the position of women among this people socially, politically and religiously.

27.4.11.en: Raamah or Raama: Raamah the son of Cush, father of Sheba and Dedan (Gen 10:7)...

27.4.12.en: It is difficult to determine the location of Raamah, whose inhabitants are thought to be of the descendants of Raamah or Raama; some thought it to be Ptolemy’s Rhegma, west of the Persian Gulf, and others see it as Rammaitae in southern Arabia, northwest of Hadramaut and east of ancient Sheba, and this last opinion is the more probable.

27.4.13.en: Haran (Charran): the name is perhaps of Akkadian origin, meaning “road” or “caravan.” The city lies northwest of al-Massisa (Mesopotamia), on the River Balikh, a tributary of the Euphrates, about 280 miles northeast of Damascus, and 60 miles east of Carchemish (Gen 11:31-32). It is considered the meeting point of one of the main roads between Babylon and the coast of the Mediterranean, and represents an important commercial center; it was the chief center for the worship of the god Sim, the moon god.

27.4.14.en: Terah and Abraham sojourned in it for a time, and Nahor settled in it, and therefore it was called by his name (Gen 42:10; 27:43). The Assyrians seized it (2 Kgs 19:12). It is at present a small village that still keeps the name Haran.

27.4.15.en: Canneh: some scholars thought it to be “Calneh” (Amos 6:2), but it is more probably an unknown Akkadian city “Kannu,” most probably in the region of al-Massisa (Mesopotamia) near Haran.

27.4.16.en: Eden: a Hebrew name meaning “delight,” and it is different from the Garden of Eden. A province of Mesopotamia, mentioned in the Assyrian inscriptions as Bit Adini, south of Haran, at the middle of the River Euphrates.

27.5.0.en: 25 “The ships of Tarshish did sing of thee in thy market: and thou wast replenished, and made very glorious in the midst of the seas. 26 Thy rowers have brought thee into great waters: the east wind hath broken thee in the midst of the seas. 27 Thy riches, and thy fairs, thy merchandise, thy mariners, and thy pilots, thy calkers, and the occupiers of thy merchandise, and all thy men of war, that are in thee, and in all thy company which is in the midst of thee, shall fall into the midst of the seas in the day of thy ruin. 28 The suburbs shall shake at the sound of the cry of thy pilots. 29 And all that handle the oar, the mariners, and all the pilots of the sea, shall come down from their ships, they shall stand upon the land; 30 And shall cause their voice to be heard against thee, and shall cry bitterly, and shall cast up dust upon their heads, they shall wallow themselves in the ashes: 31 And they shall make themselves utterly bald for thee, and gird them with sackcloth, and they shall weep for thee with bitterness of heart and bitter wailing. 32 And in their wailing they shall take up a lamentation for thee, and lament over thee, saying, What city is like Tyrus, like the destroyed in the midst of the sea? 33 When thy wares went forth out of the seas, thou filledst many people; thou didst enrich the kings of the earth with the multitude of thy riches and of thy merchandise. 34 In the time when thou shalt be broken by the seas in the depths of the waters thy merchandise and all thy company in the midst of thee shall fall. 35 All the inhabitants of the isles shall be astonished at thee, and their kings shall be sore afraid, they shall be troubled in their countenance. 36 The merchants among the people shall hiss at thee; thou shalt be a terror, and never shalt be any more.”

27.6.0.en: Tyre had become like a huge ship, perfect in its construction, strong in its guards, experienced and wise in its crew, loved by all the peoples who deal with her and seek her favor; but since she coveted and wanted to plunder her sister “Judah” on the day of her captivity, an east wind broke her and brought her down to the depths together with her wealth, her goods, her crew, her customers and her guards... There was no one to rescue and no one to help; many stood in grief and bitterness, they shaved their heads and made themselves bald like one mourning for the dead, and made a lamentation over her who used to satisfy them with good things [33]; they were in bitterness and their kings shuddered, while some stood hissing at her in mockery because she coveted and lost even her existence forever!

27.6.1.en: Steer the ship of my life!

27.6.2.en: * “Tyre,” the great city, is a ship made by Your hands; You are its maker, and You are the giver to it of every wealth, but she trusted in her riches, and resisted Your work, and so was utterly shattered!!

27.6.3.en: * I am Your ship, O my Creator!

27.6.4.en: Steer the ship of my life, for I am the work of Your hands!

27.6.5.en: * What are these boards of fir but the members of my body?!

27.6.6.en: They are Your beautiful creation; You gave me the body with the soul that they may glorify You!

27.6.7.en: Sanctify my eyes and all my senses that they may be satisfied with You!

27.6.8.en: Sanctify my emotions and my feelings, O desire of my heart!

27.6.9.en: My body is in Your hands; it is Your precious gift to me!

27.6.10.en: * What is this mast of the cedars of Lebanon which You have set up in me but the wonderful mind?!

27.6.11.en: You created it upright that it may be occupied with You throughout the journey of my short life!

27.6.12.en: My mind contemplates Your will, and so desires obedience to Your commandment, seeing in it the sweetness of fellowship with You, O Source of life!

27.6.13.en: * What is this little oar that moves all my life but the tongue?!

27.6.14.en: Sanctify it, that it may not blaspheme You, nor curse anyone, nor move in vain without purpose!

27.6.15.en: Steer it, that it may bless You and praise You and thank You continually, and bless people and overflow with sweetness to everyone!

27.6.16.en: * What are these benches of inlaid ivory but the pure senses You gave me?!

27.6.17.en: May You satisfy them with Your Holy Spirit, that they may see You, the heavenly Bridegroom of the soul, and be set aflame with love for You and for all Your creation! They are not a theater for demons, nor a pleasure-ground for fleshly desires!

27.6.18.en: My senses and my emotions and all my feelings are for You, O Beloved!

27.6.19.en: * What is this sail of embroidered linen but my little heart to which You gave purity?!

27.6.20.en: By Your Holy Spirit it grows wide to hold Him whom heaven and earth cannot contain!

27.6.21.en: Its keys are in Your hands, O Son of David, that You may enter and sup in it, and gather in it Your friends, heavenly and earthly, and establish from it Your joyful Kingdom and Your holy temple!

27.6.22.en: * What are these coverings of the ship of my life but the conduct which I practice by the work of Your grace?!

27.6.23.en: It is of blue, bearing the color of heaven, and of purple, the garment of kings.

27.6.24.en: You are wonderful, O heavenly King of kings, for You want me in my conduct to bear Your marks, to walk on earth with a heavenly heart, and to live in the narrowness of the world as a king possessing authority!

27.6.25.en: * Who are the mariners of Zidon but the inner energies of the soul?!

27.6.26.en: Grant them to be skilled hunters, working always for the edification of my soul and the edification of my brethren, knowing neither demolition nor destruction!

27.6.27.en: You gave me wonderful energies like spiritual soldiers; steer them to work on behalf of Your Kingdom, that they may not be wicked soldiers on behalf of the kingdom of darkness!

27.6.28.en: * Who is this pilot from Tyre but the spirit of discernment and distinction?!

27.6.29.en: He is the gift of Your Holy Spirit; by him I recognize the good and distinguish it from evil, by him I do not deviate from Your royal way to the right or to the left!

27.6.30.en: Self-righteousness does not deceive me, nor do desires draw me away!

27.6.31.en: By him I come to know You, O Truth!

27.6.32.en: * Who are the calkers but the gifts which You entrusted to me?!

27.6.33.en: Kindle, O Lord, Your gifts in me, that I may work with power and wisdom!

27.6.34.en: May I work in harmony and accord with the gifts of my brethren, without pride and without smallness of soul.

27.6.35.en: I thank You for giving me the gifts that suit me!

27.6.36.en: * Who are these guards from Persia, Lud and Phut but the drives which You created in me!

27.6.37.en: By the drive of love I meet You and love Your creation!

27.6.38.en: By the drive of anger I rise against my sin and complain to You of myself!

27.6.39.en: By the drive of fear I fear You in love!

27.6.40.en: Sanctify all the drives so that they deviate no more!

27.6.41.en: * Wretched is Tyre, the beautiful, rich ship, which trusted in herself and disobeyed her Creator, so she was shattered and sank in the sea of this world!

27.6.42.en: * Steer, O wonderful Captain, the ship of my life; let Your Cross be the mast of my life, and Your commandments the sailors!

27.6.43.en: Grant me ropes to support my ship.

27.6.44.en: I am in the midst of the currents of the sea of this world, but I am carried by Your Holy Spirit to the heavenly harbor!
